stem: Line $L$ has equation $y = {=linear(m0, b0)}$. Draw the line through the point $({=px}, {=py})$ that is {=relation} to $L$.
solution: Read the gradient of L from its equation (the coefficient of x).
Apply the rule for the relationship asked: parallel keeps the same gradient; perpendicular takes the negative reciprocal.
Substitute the given point's coordinates into y = mx + c with the new gradient and solve for c.
Draw the line with that gradient through the given point (or any other point lying on it).
notes:
Tests the 'use the relationship to find the equation of a line' half of LO2. Verified numerically for both instances (reference gradients 2 and -3, neither ±1) that applying the wrong relationship produces a gradient matching neither slope-inverted nor slope-sign-flipped against the true target, so it lands cleanly on off-target — mapped to this LO's own swaps-parallel-perpendicular-tests, the likeliest error and the one this construction most specifically reveals. The remaining predicates surface LO1 prerequisite slips (own=false) that a construction can't tell apart from a genuine relationship confusion once only the resulting line is observed. vertical-line has no match here. This LO's other three misconceptions (judges-parallel-by-appearance, stops-at-partial-quadrilateral-property, and swaps-parallel-perpendicular-tests read as a classification act rather than a construction act) describe judging an already-given relationship or shape, not drawing a fresh line — see the filed gap for this LO.
